title: The Sugar That Stayed After the Milk Was Gone — Classic Galactosemia, GALT Ping-Pong His186 Catalysis (5IN3), Endogenous [1-13C]Galactose Production & Aldose Reductase

teenKit.tldr: Babies with classic galactosemia can't process milk sugar due to a jammed cellular factory machine, but cutting dairy isn't enough because human bodies manufacture their own internal supply.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our cells secretly build their own biochemical roadblocks reveals why fixing genetic diseases takes much more than simply changing what we eat.
keyTakeaways: Classic galactosemia happens when the GALT enzyme jams up, stopping the body from breaking down a specific type of sugar found in milk.
Even when babies completely stop eating dairy, brilliant isotope-tracer experiments prove their bodies still manufacture about one gram of galactose internally every single day.
An alternate enzyme called aldose reductase converts this leftover internal sugar into galactitol, which causes long-term complications despite strict diets.

vocab.meaning: A rare genetic condition where the body cannot properly break down galactose, a simple sugar found in milk.
The specific molecular machine responsible for the crucial second step of converting galactose into usable cellular energy.
A modified atom used like a tiny glowing GPS tracker to follow specific chemical pathways through the human body.
A backup enzyme that forces leftover galactose to turn into a sugar-alcohol called galactitol instead of clearing it out.

quiz.question: Why do infants with classic galactosemia experience severe crisis when consuming regular milk?
options: Their stomachs cannot produce enough acid to curdle milk proteins.
Their GALT enzyme is broken, causing toxic milk sugars and byproducts to back up in their cells.
They are severely allergic to the fat molecules floating in mammalian milk.
Their bodies instantly destroy all available lactose without absorbing any nutrients.
quiz.explanation: A jammed GALT enzyme stops the metabolic assembly line, causing a toxic pileup of unprocessed sugar intermediates.

quiz.question: What did the Berry et al. stable isotope tracer study reveal about the human body?
options: Human bodies naturally manufacture about one gram of endogenous galactose daily even with zero dairy intake.
The human liver completely stops producing any sugars after the first year of life.
Dietary galactose is entirely converted into pure water and carbon dioxide within minutes.
Cellular factories can completely bypass broken enzymes by building entirely new molecular pathways.
quiz.explanation: Isotope tracking proved that cutting out dietary dairy doesn't stop the body from synthesizing its own internal galactose.

quiz.question: What role does aldose reductase play in the long-term complications of galactosemia?
options: It successfully repairs the broken GALT enzyme during adolescent growth spurts.
It helps the kidneys flush out excess sugar molecules safely through urine.
It converts leftover internal galactose into galactitol, which can accumulate and cause long-term cellular damage.
It blocks milk sugars from ever entering sensitive tissues like the ovaries and brain.
quiz.explanation: Aldose reductase acts on the trapped internal galactose, turning it into galactitol which drives long-term complications.
